item.title: Can Keeping a Journal Make You Happier?
item.description:
Emotions

Can Keeping a Journal Make You Happier?

Writing about the bad can be good for you.

Posted August 7, 2026

Journaling can have long-term benefits
Source: Grok / xAi

Many people associate diary-keeping with the tortured musings of adolescents dealing with romantic crushes or social isolation.

There is some truth to this stereotype, since a 2023 survey by Statista found that fully one fifth of American participants aged 14 to 25 engaged in journaling to help them manage their mental health. Yet adults actually may do so at even higher rates: a 2025 YouGov survey found that only 47 percent of respondents said they “never” write about their personal thoughts.

But what makes this activity so popular? The simple answer is that it seems to make you feel better.

This intuitive belief has been the subject of much research on what researchers call expressive writing or emotional disclosure. Crucially, this refers to writing down one’s feelings and reactions as opposed to just recording the events of one’s day.

What Research Tells Us About the Benefits of Emotional Disclosure

James Pennebaker, a psychologist at the University of Texas, conducted pioneering work on this topic beginning in the 1980s. He and his collaborators asked college students to write about traumatic personal experiences for short periods across several days. Compared to a control group writing about mundane topics, those who had written about their significant emotional experiences were found to benefit in a variety of ways.

Across Pennebaker's studies, it's been demonstrated that the expressive writing participants report lower levels of distress and depression, fewer physical symptoms, and even better grades. The researchers also documented, in follow-ups with these participants, fewer visits to physicians and even long-term immune function improvements in the days and months following their expressive writing (Pennebaker, 1997).

In other words, writing about emotional events may not just make you happier—it may also make you healthier.

Researchers later combined the results of many similar studies to conduct meta-analyses of this research. Frattaroli (2006) included 146 studies in her analysis and found small but significant benefical effects for expressive writing. A later meta-analysis by Guo (2023), which included studies employing longer-term follow-ups, also reported a beneficial effect.

In 2009, UCLA psychologist Matthew Lieberman and his collaborators described a possible physiological mechanism to explain why such writing is helpful. Research participants in a neuroimaging study were asked to provide a verbal label for an affective display, such as an angry face. Compared to a control group, these participants howed greater activity in a part of the brain that dampens the neural activity associated with strong emotions (Lieberman et al., 2007).

In other words, the act of identifying or describing negative emotions may help to attenuate them.

Does Writing Always Help Us Feel Better?

It should be noted, however, that expressive writing isn’t some magical elixir. One important caveat is that, immediately after writing about traumatic events, participants in research studies frequently report feeling worse—not better.

This phenomenon was first noted by Pennebaker and Beall (1986), and several later studies have also observed this effect. Some researchers have reported that the negative feelings may persist for an hour or two—making it comparable to the short-term decline in mood after watching a sad movie.

Still, even these brief episodes of negative affect may be one of the reasons that so many people abandon journaling or keeping a diary after only a few days. This is unfortunate, because it means that they never reap the long-term benefits of writing about their feelings.

It’s also the case that people who tend to ruminate—that is, those who engage in repetitive and prolonged thinking about negative experiences—may be adversely affected by engaging in expressive writing.

A study by David Sbarra and his collaborators found that, among research participants who had recently separated from a spouse, those who scored high on a measure of rumination reported more distress following sessions in which they wrote about the dissolution of their marriage. In addition, these negative effects persisted for up to nine months following the writing sessions (Sbarra et al., 2013).

Another study found that an expressive writing intervention during the COVID-19 pandemic had the effect of elevating participants’ stress levels, and these effects were still seen at a one-month follow-up (Vukčević Marković et al., 2020). However, this result may only obtain when people are experiencing a high degree of fear or uncertainty—such as during a global health crisis.

In general, however—for most people and most of the time—writing or journaling about one’s emotional experiences can pay lasting dividends. Short-term negative effects are typically transitory, and the benefits can be long lasting.

item.title: What to Do When Experiencing Advocacy Burnout
item.description:
Burnout

What to Do When Experiencing Advocacy Burnout

Being tired of advocating doesn't make you weak... just exhausted.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Advocacy burnout occurs when your child’s needs begin to put strain on your emotional and mental resources.
  • Be mindful of advocacy burnout signs and any gradual changes in your behavior, like feelings of overwhelm.
  • Scheduling advocacy time blocks is a good way to ensure that advocacy tasks don’t consume you every day.
  • It’s OK to ask for help, leave something for another day, or say, “I can’t handle that right now.”

As the school year approaches, most parents have back-to-school shopping on their mind, helping children pick out new clothes, shoes, and backpack essentials. However, for parents of a neurodivergent child, things look, well, a bit different. Cue the list of meetings and updates you need to coordinate across teachers, therapists, and other providers to share news about your child’s progress, ongoing needs, and recent milestones and/or challenges. For any parent in this situation, this likely sounds all too familiar, and I’ll bet that at some point, you’ve already dealt with advocacy burnout.

Advocacy burnout is very real and occurs when the ongoing demands of supporting, monitoring, and seemingly fighting for your child’s needs begin to put strain on your emotional and mental resources. Although a positive action, advocacy is also never-ending. In my experience, every “successful” meeting often leads to more emails, follow-up calls, and maybe even more evaluations. When a parent feels as though they’re always working but never truly completing a task, this can lead to burnout. I mean, it feels exhausting just typing this all out!

Unlike ordinary stress, advocacy burnout for parents often develops gradually, and I see the patterns with most of my clients. Typically, it’s a longer buildup, and many don’t recognize it immediately. At first, they feel tired. Then they begin feeling overwhelmed. Eventually, they may feel emotionally depleted. Am I hitting a nerve yet?

If you think you’re experiencing advocacy burnout, here are some signs to pay attention to:

  • Are you more irritable and feeling a loss of motivation or discouragement?
  • Are you having difficulty concentrating and noticing that you’re more forgetful?
  • Are you worried? Do you find that you’re avoiding emails and phone calls and purposefully ignoring school communications and appointments?

If you answered yes to any of the above, this is likely advocacy burnout. It often means that you worry about your child and their progress; it doesn’t mean you’re weak. If I were to guess, I’d say you’re overwhelmed and exhausted and have nothing left to give. And honestly, no parent can say they’ve never been pulled in several different directions.

As a parent advocate, you need to protect yourself from burnout, or you won’t be able to care for your child as best as you can. Here are a few reminders I often discuss with my clients:

Set realistic goals for yourself. You’re a person with feelings and emotions, not a machine. That said, not every teacher or therapist will value you; accept that, even when it feels frustrating. But don’t give up or go quiet to minimize confrontation when facing a difference of opinion with others. Parents are responsible for advocacy, but they’re not responsible for controlling every outcome.

Surround yourself with supportive family and friends. It’s ok to complain, vent, and just let it out when you’re annoyed and frustrated. Someone who has been through the same experience, or even something similar, can often provide a bit of validation to get you through a challenging day.

Build yourself a management system. Create a calendar, share it with others, and build a file of documents and reminders. You don’t have to remember everything on your own. Also, stop trying to solve every problem immediately. Not every issue requires immediate action. Before responding, ask yourself: Is this urgent? Do I need more information? You can even schedule advocacy time blocks, so advocacy tasks don’t consume every free moment of your life.

Celebrate progress, not just problems. Burnout often develops because parents focus exclusively on challenges. Start tracking wins, even small ones such as improved reading, better emotional regulation, increased independence, and positive teacher feedback. Without recognizing victories, advocacy can feel like ongoing crisis management.

A big myth noted in advocacy: “If I care enough, I can handle everything.” I’m here to tell you: No, you can’t and you shouldn’t, no matter how much you care about your child.

It’s ok to ask for help, leave something for another day, or say, “I can’t handle that right now.” You don’t have to operate in hero mode 24/7, and even heroes deserve a break.

item.title: The New Five-Step-No-Tiger Method to Reduce Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

The New Five-Step-No-Tiger Method to Reduce Anxiety

Why your Stone-Age brain overreacts to modern threats—and how to calm it.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Sometimes, our anxiety feels far more intense than the situation seems to justify.
  • That's because our brain often reacts to modern stressors as if a predator were just around the corner.
  • Learn five practical steps to quiet the ancient survival instincts driving unnecessary anxiety.
Source: AI-Generated/ChatGPT

Do criticism, uncertainty, health concerns, financial setbacks, relationship problems, or personal losses trigger anxiety that feels far more intense than the situation seems to justify?

If so, the problem may not be weakness, lack of willpower, or faulty thinking.

The problem may be that your brain is doing exactly what it evolved to do in the harsh environments of our ancestors.

Case scenario of a patient with excessive anxiety

Because Sylvia’s mother died of stomach cancer, Sylvia became extremely anxious about getting the same cancer. Despite numerous endoscopies, blood tests, and CT scans showing no abnormalities, Sylvia’s anxiety grew to the point that she couldn’t get any restful sleep anymore.

Constantly worried, she discovered that snacking calmed her anxiety. She became obese, hypertensive, and diabetic. Her anxious body, hard-wired by the constant food scarcity of her ancestors to fear starvation, pushed her to stuff herself with food and do as little physical exercise as possible to conserve energy.

A vicious circle emerged where obesity, high blood pressure, and diabetes elevated her risk of a heart attack, cancer, and death. Awareness of this led her to be more anxious, which led her to eat more, etc.

Where did Sylvia’s excessive anxiety come from?

Evolutionary roots of excessive anxiety

Sylvia had every reason to be anxious about getting cancer, but her anxiety, given that all her tests were normal, was inappropriate and destroying her health. How could she change that?

A new book, written by Psychology Today blogger Eric Haseltine, Ph.D., and me, called There’s No Tiger Around That Corner: How Your Stone-Aged Brain Makes You Overanxious and What to Do About It, shows the “five-step-no-tiger” method that helped Sylvia turn a vicious circle into a virtuous one. [1]

In this book, we show that our modern brains retain ancient hunter-gatherer survival programs which create a mismatch between modern situations and ancient reactions to ancient threats.

This idea comes from evolutionary psychology: For hundreds of thousands of years, our ancestors faced predators, starvation, disease, violence, social rejection, and other threats that could have catastrophic consequences. To survive, the human brain evolved powerful threat-detection systems designed to anticipate danger and prepare for the worst. Those ancient systems still operate today. [2] [3]

The result is that modern stressors can trigger emotions calibrated for a much harsher world.

Our brain sees a tiger when, most of the time, there isn’t one.

In Sylvia’s case, she was excessively worried about stomach cancer and starvation (possible tigers around the corner), which in ancient times could have killed her, but which in modern times, with proper regular medical surveillance and awareness of food availability, was nothing to lose sleep over.

How did Sylvia dial back her extreme anxiety? With our “five-step-no-tiger” method.

Reducing excess anxiety using the “five-step-no-tiger” method

1. Follow anxiety to its roots.

Where does your intense anxiety really come from?

In Sylvia’s case, anxiety reduction began by getting her to acknowledge that she perceived any threat, however imaginary, as existential. Given her tests, the probability that stomach cancer would kill her was very low, but her brain’s ancient programs—including a strong negativity bias—amplified that very low probability into a high one.

Starvation was indeed a real threat in ancient times, but in modern times, food is abundant, so Sylvia didn’t have to stuff herself, nor conserve energy by not exercising.

2. Talk to both your ancient brain and your modern brain.

In Sylvia’s case, step two adapted CBT self-talk techniques to persuade the primitive part of her brain that her life wasn’t about to end. For this, she used images like an annoying skunk around the corner instead of a deadly tiger.

Sylvia also talked to her modern brain, using rational data to increase her awareness of the situation: “All my tests are normal, so I don’t have to worry right now. Worrying pushes me to snack all the time, harming my health. I don’t have to worry about starvation, so I can eat less and start exercising. That will decrease my cancer risk.”

3. Know what to expect.

Expect setbacks. The road to feeling better will not be a straight line up. There will be ups and downs, successes and setbacks. Humans are not perfect, and Sylvia understood that all she had to do was do the best she could with what she had.

4. Notice and celebrate small victories.

If Sylvia delayed eating for 10 minutes, if she had a smaller portion of food one day, if she went for a short walk, if she lost one pound, if she felt slightly less frightened one day, those were small victories worth noticing and celebrating. This is how she rebuilt trust in herself.

5. Use setbacks instead of being defeated by them.

Sylvia accepted that setbacks were going to happen, so the key to her success was to learn from her setbacks rather than be defeated by them.

Eric and I have used our “five-step-no-tiger” method successfully to reduce our own intense anxieties and to help therapy clients and our anxious patients, respectively.

We have learned and are now teaching how to bring unconscious, primitive beliefs into the cold light of modern reality so that those primitive beliefs can be critically examined, then reframed.

Reframing and managing both your primitive brain and your modern brain will allow you to live a healthier, happier, and longer life.
